newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Military abuses drive Filipinos to rebel arms - study.
newsitem.headline: Military abuses drive Filipinos to rebel arms - study.

text.p: A government-commissioned study cited military abuses as the main factor that drives Filipinos to take up arms and join communist rebels, according to results of the study made available on Tuesday.

The study, based on interviews with 171 of 2,461 former guerrillas granted amnesty by the government, also found that 95 percent had decided to return to the national mainstream because they felt demoralised with the rebel movement.
Only 5.3 percent abandoned the revolution because they wanted to live again peacefully with their families, the study showed.
The results imply it was not the attraction of peace but "frustration with the communist movement itself" that spurred most of them to lay down their arms, said the study.
A total of 126 respondents, or 73.68 percent, cited abuses by the military and police in their communities as the main reason they had joined the rebel New People's Army (NPA), the study said.
Twenty-one, or 12.28 percent, cited poverty as reason while 18, or 10.52 percent, said they went to the mountains because they believed in the communist ideology.

The study, conducted by a lawyer and a consultant to a government panel negotiating peace with the guerrillas, indicated most of the former rebels "may not have completely renounced armed struggle as a means for social change".
"Given the proper motivation and under the right conditions, (they) may take up arms again," it said.

The government estimates current NPA strength at about 6,000 men, sharply down from the peak of about 27,000 in the late 1980s. It attributes the decline to the collapse of communism in Europe, disputes within rebel ranks, battlefield losses and defections.
